name: Mike Zheng Shou

papers.title: Where Success Breaks: Failure-Boundary Learning for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapted through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) inherit a structural asymmetry: expert demonstrations teach the policy where success behavior lies, but provide no signal about where it ceases to be reliable.
We argue that robust VLA adaptation should therefore be viewed not as further demonstration fitting, but as \textbf{Failure-Boundary Learning}---the problem of \textit{\textbf{D}iscovering}, \textit{\textbf{L}ocalizing}, and \textit{\textbf{S}haping} the boundary between recoverable deviations and task failure. To instantiate this view, we propose \textbf{\textit{DLS}}: built on a \textbf{\textit{real-grounded behavioral prior}} from few real demonstrations and simulated co-training, DLS \textit{discovers} failure boundaries at scale through on-policy digital twin rollouts. Rather than reducing each rollout to a binary label, \textbf{\textit{semantic progress localization}} uses privileged simulator states to assign progress-aware signals that capture \textit{where} the failure boundary is crossed, not merely \textit{whether}. These signals drive \textbf{\textit{directional boundary shaping}} in the flow dynamics---reinforcing success-producing denoising directions and suppressing failure-producing ones, without action likelihoods or auxiliary critics. Across real-robot manipulation tasks, DLS improves robustness over SFT and online RL baselines, especially under randomized initial states and unseen visual conditions.

papers.title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
papers.abstract:
Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g., proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders.
We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less.
Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks.

papers.title: Supervise What Survives: Geometry-Guided VLA Adaptation from Synthetic Robot Videos
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models require large-scale video-action pairs, yet real teleoperation remains scarce. While generated robot videos offer a scalable alternative, existing methods treat them as real robot data by recovering pseudo-actions from synthesized pixels. We argue that deriving low-level control from generated visuals is a mismatched abstraction. A video captures only geometry: the spatial trajectory representing the where of a task. A real demonstration captures control: the exact motor commands representing the how. Human-to-robot video generation preserves these unequally: the visible geometry survives the generation process, while the underlying control signals are lost. This Asymmetric Preservation Principle dictates a clean rule: this surviving geometry should solely supervise visual perception, leaving control to real demonstrations. Following this principle, we propose GRA (Geometry-guided Representation Alignment), which extracts the geometric content as future 2D end-effector waypoints, computed from the source human video through pose estimation, retargeting, simulation, and calibrated projection, and routes them to the VLA vision backbone via an auxiliary 2D head. The action head is trained on real demonstrations only. During fine-tuning, the waypoint loss persists as a spatial representation anchor that prevents the backbone from losing its geometric grounding. On real-robot tasks, GRA outperforms pseudo-action baselines under matched data budgets and narrows the gap to policies trained with substantially more real demonstrations, suggesting that correctly routed geometry bridges generated videos to robot policies more reliably than recovered actions.
